sections.body:
# Agent Architecture

To attack an agent effectively, you first have to understand how it's actually put together. An agent isn't one single thing. It's several distinct parts working together as a team.

## The five core components

| Component | Simple meaning | Real-world analogy |
|-----------|----------------|--------------------|
| LLM (brain) | Understands language and decides what to do | The employee's mind |
| Instructions | The system prompt that sets rules and goals | The job description |
| Tools | Functions the agent can call | The employee's hands and equipment |
| Memory | Stores past events and facts | The employee's notebook |
| Orchestrator | The code that runs the loop | The office manager |

The orchestrator is important and often overlooked entirely. The LLM doesn't actually run tools by itself. The LLM only outputs text saying something like "I want to call tool X with these inputs." The orchestrator, which is just normal code you wrote, reads that text and actually runs the tool on the LLM's behalf.

This gap between deciding and doing is a genuine security goldmine, and we'll return to it many times throughout this module.

sections.body:
## How a single turn actually flows

1. The user sends input to the orchestrator.
2. The orchestrator builds a full prompt: system instructions plus memory plus the tool list plus the user's input.
3. The LLM reads this and replies. That reply is either a final answer or a tool call request.
4. If it's a tool call, the orchestrator actually runs the real underlying function.
5. The tool's result gets added back into the ongoing conversation.
6. Steps 3 through 5 repeat until the LLM finally produces a proper final answer.

## The critical realization

Everything the LLM sees is just one large block of text. The system instructions, the memory, the tool results, and the user input are all mixed together into the same shared context.

The LLM has no reliable way to truly distinguish "this part is a trusted rule from the developer" from "this part is untrusted text pulled from some random website." To the model, it's genuinely all just text.

That single fact is the root cause of nearly every agent vulnerability covered in this module.

**Look closely at the code.** Tool output goes straight back into the context. If a tool fetches an attacker-controlled web page, the attacker's text is now sitting inside the agent's "mind," carrying the exact same status as everything else in that context. This is precisely how indirect attacks against agents begin.

## Key takeaways

- An agent equals an LLM plus instructions plus tools plus memory plus an orchestrator.
- The orchestrator, not the LLM itself, is what actually executes tools.
- The LLM sees everything as one single text blob and can't reliably separate trusted content from untrusted content.
- Tool results re-enter the shared context, meaning external data effectively becomes part of the agent's own reasoning process.
